title: Darolutamide: high-risk nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
indication_text: Castration-resistant prostate cancer with no metastases detected on conventional imaging and a high risk of developing metastases, as defined in NCCP regimen 00693.
purpose: This treatment aims to control prostate cancer and delay progression. The expected benefit depends on your disease setting, previous treatment and general health.
cycle_display: Twice daily with food plus ongoing ADT
schedule_label: Twice daily with food plus ongoing ADT
schedule_summary: Darolutamide 600 mg twice daily with food, continuously while helping and tolerated. Continue ADT unless surgically castrated. The team may prescribe 300 mg twice daily for selected organ impairment or toxicity.
administration_text: Take the morning and evening doses with food; swallow tablets whole with water. Take a missed dose when remembered before the next scheduled dose, then return to the normal schedule. Do not take two doses together or double the dose. Confirm any prescribed reduction with your team.
monitoring_summary: Repeat blood count, kidney and liver tests on your agreed schedule; blood pressure and ECG as clinically indicated. The NCCP regimen does not give a universal blood-test or scan interval. Monitor more closely with kidney or liver impairment.

agents.name: Darolutamide
agents.explanation: Darolutamide blocks the androgen receptor and its growth signals. It adds to continued ADT to reduce the risk of progression in this particular high-risk nonmetastatic setting.
agents.watch: Ask pharmacy to check all medicines, especially cholesterol medicines such as rosuvastatin and enzyme-inducing medicines or herbal products. Report jaundice, dark urine, severe tiredness, chest symptoms or a marked change in wellbeing promptly.
risks: Rash, limb pain and changes in blood counts or liver blood tests
Ischaemic heart disease or heart failure
Interactions, including increased exposure to some cholesterol medicines
Hot flushes, sexual or fertility effects and bone loss with ongoing ADT

anatomy: Report troublesome fatigue, falls or confusion. Seizure, collapse or sudden neurological symptoms need emergency help.
Ask about help for hot flushes, mood changes, sleep and daily activity. Keep your ADT appointments.
Keep blood-pressure checks. Chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness needs urgent help; report ankle swelling or palpitations.
Keep liver blood tests. Report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced appetite or a major change in wellbeing.
Report persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, inability to drink or take medicines, and unintended weight loss.
Report a new rash. Severe rash with blisters, peeling, fever or mouth/eye sores needs urgent assessment.
Discuss erections, libido, fertility and contraception. Avoid exposing a pregnant partner to these medicines; follow the product-specific precautions.
Discuss bone-density assessment, falls prevention, suitable resistance and aerobic activity, calcium intake and vitamin D needs.

items.title: Who this treatment is for
items.text: Castration-resistant prostate cancer with no metastases detected on conventional imaging and a high risk of developing metastases, as defined in NCCP regimen 00693.

items.title: Specialist tests
items.text: NCCP selection includes PSA at least 2 ng/mL, PSA doubling time no more than 10 months and testosterone below 1.7 nmol/L. PSA, symptoms and appropriate scans are interpreted together.

items.title: Why ADT continues
items.text: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) lowers testosterone from the testes. This medicine adds another form of hormone-pathway blockade. Even when cancer becomes castration-resistant, continued testosterone suppression remains part of this treatment unless you have had surgical castration.

items.title: Prescribed treatment
items.text: Darolutamide 600 mg twice daily with food, continuously while helping and tolerated. Continue ADT unless surgically castrated. The team may prescribe 300 mg twice daily for selected organ impairment or toxicity.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Repeat blood count, kidney and liver tests on your agreed schedule; blood pressure and ECG as clinically indicated. The NCCP regimen does not give a universal blood-test or scan interval. Monitor more closely with kidney or liver impairment.

items.title: Deciding together
items.text: This treatment aims to slow cancer growth and help control symptoms. Your team explains the expected benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for your situation.

items.title: Review and alternatives
items.text: Continue your prescribed androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), unless you have had surgery to remove both testes. The team reviews symptoms, blood tests, PSA and scans according to your own plan; there is no universal scan interval. Discuss suitable alternatives, supportive care and the option of declining treatment.

items.title: Where radiotherapy fits
items.text: Radiotherapy may treat the prostate, a recurrence or a troublesome site such as a painful bone lesion. Its purpose depends on your disease setting. Ask the team whether it belongs in your plan; starting these tablets does not itself schedule or replace radiotherapy.

evidence.title: What the evidence can tell you
evidence.intro: Research supports a treatment discussion; it cannot predict one person’s outcome.
evidence.population: Castration-resistant prostate cancer with no metastases detected on conventional imaging and a high risk of developing metastases, as defined in NCCP regimen 00693.
evidence.comparison: The exact comparison and population stated below; no comparison across trials is implied.
evidence.interpretation: In ARAMIS, adding darolutamide to continued ADT increased median time to metastasis or death to 40.4 months versus 18.4 months with placebo plus ADT (HR 0.41; 95% CI 0.34–0.50). This is not a promise of an extra 22 months of life. Metastatic darolutamide combinations are a separate indication and are not included in this NCCP 00693 patient service.
limitations: Trial populations and schedules differ; comparisons across separate trials are unreliable.
An improvement in progression-free survival is not automatically an overall-survival benefit.
